\subsection{Registration and Scalar-on-Function Regression: Tecator Data}
\label{subsec:cs2-tecator}

The tecator dataset consists of 240 near-infrared absorbance spectra of meat
samples measured at 100 spectral channels, with fat content (ranging from
0.9\% to 58.5\%) recorded as a scalar response for each sample
\citep{ramsay_silverman_2005}.  The spectra exhibit phase variability —
curves that carry the same shape but are shifted or compressed along the
spectral axis — which motivates a registration step before regression.
This study demonstrates two additional \texttt{fdars} capabilities:
elastic curve registration via the square-root velocity framework
\citep{srivastava_klassen_2016} and scalar-on-function FPC regression
\citep{preda_saporta_2005}.

\paragraph{Registration.}
We estimate an elastic Karcher mean from a representative subset of 30 curves
using \texttt{fdars.alignment.karcher\_mean} (Fisher--Rao gradient descent,
capped at 20 iterations) and then align all 240 spectra to that mean with
\texttt{fdars.alignment.align\_to\_target}.  The iteration cap is chosen for
computational efficiency; convergence is not required for the registration to
be illustrative \citep{srivastava_klassen_2016}.
Figure~\ref{fig:cs2-align} shows the 30 raw spectra (grey) alongside their
registered counterparts and the Karcher mean (highlighted), revealing how
elastic alignment reduces phase dispersion while preserving the characteristic
spectral peaks.

\paragraph{Scalar-on-function regression.}
Fat content is modelled as a linear functional of the spectral curve via FPC
regression implemented in \texttt{fdars.regression.fregre\_lm} with five
functional principal components \citep{preda_saporta_2005}.  Fitting on all
240 samples yields a training $R^2 = 0.929$, confirming that the first five
spectral modes of variation explain the dominant share of fat-content variance.
Figure~\ref{fig:cs2-fit} plots actual against fitted fat content; the scatter
follows the diagonal closely throughout the range, with the reference line
$y = x$ shown for comparison.

\paragraph{Cross-validation.}
To assess generalisation, we evaluate \texttt{FPCRegressor} (5 components)
via 5-fold cross-validation using
\texttt{sklearn.\allowbreak model\_selection.\allowbreak cross\_val\_score}.
The fold-level $R^2$ scores are $[0.903, 0.405, 0.883, 0.922, 0.914]$,
giving a mean CV $R^2 = 0.805$.  The weak second fold (0.405) reflects genuine
variability in held-out performance; the mean is reported without adjustment.
The complete analysis is reproduced deterministically by
\texttt{paper/code/casestudy2.py}, which writes both figures via the
\texttt{paper\_utils.save\_figure} harness (re-running the script leaves
\texttt{git diff paper/figures/} empty).

    Bold trace: estimated Karcher mean used as the registration target
